input.text_to_find: However, there were still limitations in our study

input.line_text: However, several limitations of our study should be acknowledged. First, indirect costs were estimated using the human capital approach, which does not account for the costs of premature retirement caused by RA or for intangible costs; this may have led to an underestimation of indirect costs. Second, RA patients frequently had multiple comorbidities, not all of which were RA-related. Because we captured their total annual healthcare spending, our per-patient costs may overestimate the costs attributable solely to RA. Third, cost estimates relied on patient self-reported data, which are subject to recall bias. To maximize accuracy, we invited only patients whose clinical records had been updated by their clinicians within the previous 30 days, and we asked participants to recall in detail the expense information of that recent visit and the frequency of visits over the past year. In addition, at the initial stage, 53 patients were randomly selected to provide information twice within two weeks so that the agreement of the reported information could be assessed. Fourth, given the cross-sectional design, we could not exclude the possibility of reverse causation or residual confounding. The observed associations between the influencing factors and RA expenditure therefore warrant confirmation in further prospective cohort studies. Finally, given an overall response rate of only 7%, our cross-sectional study was susceptible to non-response bias. Although IPW mitigated imbalances in observed characteristics, residual confounding from unmeasured factors (such as income and health-seeking behaviors) may persist, which could limit the external validity of our findings for the broader RA population.
